title: Given a directed acyclic graph of dependencies, produce a linear ordering of the nodes such that every edge points from an earlier node to a later node. Explain the Topological Sort pattern using Kahn's algorithm, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Topological Sort (Linear Ordering of a Directed Acyclic Graph)

s1_definition.profdef: Topological Sort is the foundational problem of the Topological Sort pattern. Using Kahn's algorithm we compute the in-degree of every node, start a queue with all zero in-degree nodes, and repeatedly remove a node and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees, enqueuing any that reach zero. The order of removal is a valid topological order. This runs in linear time in the number of nodes and edges.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a set of end-of-day batch jobs where some jobs must finish before others can start, and it needs a safe run order so no job starts before its prerequisites. Topological Sort finds that order by always running the jobs that currently have no pending prerequisites.
s1_definition.oneliner: Repeatedly take any node with no remaining prerequisites, output it, and relax its outgoing edges.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Topological Sort is the foundational problem of the Topological Sort pattern. Using Kahn's algorithm we compute the in-degree of every node, start a queue with all zero in-degree nodes, and repeatedly remove a node and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees, enqueuing any that reach zero. The order of removal is a valid topological order. This runs in linear time in the number of nodes and edges.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a set of end-of-day batch jobs where some jobs must finish before others can start, and it needs a safe run order so no job starts before its prerequisites. Topological Sort finds that order by always running the jobs that currently have no pending prerequisites.

**One line to remember:** Repeatedly take any node with no remaining prerequisites, output it, and relax its outgoing edges.

sections.s2_technical:
Kahn's algorithm models prerequisites as directed edges from a prerequisite to its dependent. The in-degree of a node is how many prerequisites still point at it. We build the adjacency list and the in-degree array, then enqueue every node with in-degree zero, because those have no prerequisites and can go first. We repeatedly remove a node from the queue, append it to the order, and for each neighbour reduce its in-degree by one, enqueuing the neighbour when its in-degree falls to zero because all its prerequisites are now placed.

The core loop is `while (!queue.isEmpty()) { int node = queue.poll(); order.add(node); for (int next : adj.get(node)) if (--indeg[next] == 0) queue.add(next); }`. If the final order contains fewer nodes than exist, the graph has a cycle and no topological order is possible. A concrete check: with job A before B and B before C, the order is A, B, C. Senior nuance: this is linear time in nodes plus edges, a depth-first variant pushes nodes onto a stack in post-order, and a shortfall in the output count is the standard cycle detector.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs end-of-day batch jobs where interest posting must precede statement generation, and statement generation must precede archival, so the operations team needs a safe linear run order that never starts a job before its prerequisites. Guessing an order risks running a job too early. This is exactly how Topological Sort works: it produces a valid dependency-respecting order with Kahn's algorithm.

The code defines a `BatchOrderService` exposing `runOrder(jobCount, dependencies)` returning the ordered list of job indices. A `Demo` builds a small dependency set and logs the order.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three jobs with dependencies that job zero precedes job one and job one precedes job two. We want a safe run order.

Step 1 — We build the adjacency list, so job zero points to job one and job one points to job two, and we compute in-degrees: job zero has zero, job one has one, job two has one.

Step 2 — We enqueue every job with in-degree zero. Only job zero qualifies, so the queue holds job zero.

Step 3 — We remove job zero, append it to the order, and relax its edge to job one, dropping job one's in-degree to zero, so job one enters the queue.

Step 4 — We remove job one, append it, and relax its edge to job two, dropping job two's in-degree to zero, so job two enters the queue.

Step 5 — We remove job two and append it. The order is job zero, job one, job two, and its size equals the job count so there is no cycle. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 9:39:48 PM com.bank.batchorder.service.BatchOrderService runOrder
INFO: Topological run order = [0, 1, 2]
Oct 27, 2026 9:39:48 PM com.bank.batchorder.BatchOrderApplication main
INFO: Safe batch run order: [0, 1, 2]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: jobs=3, deps = 0→1, 1→2
    │
    ▼
  in-degrees: job0=0, job1=1, job2=1
    │ queue: [0]  (only zero in-degree)
    │ poll 0 → order[0]; relax 0→1 → job1 indeg 0 → enqueue
    │ poll 1 → order[1]; relax 1→2 → job2 indeg 0 → enqueue
    │ poll 2 → order[2]
    ▼
  Output: run order = [0, 1, 2]  (size == jobCount, no cycle)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Topological Sort is the foundational problem of the Topological Sort pattern, and I solve it with Kahn's algorithm, which is a breadth-first approach driven by in-degrees. I model each prerequisite as a directed edge from the prerequisite to its dependent, and the in-degree of a node counts how many prerequisites still point at it. I build the adjacency list and the in-degree array, then start a queue with every node whose in-degree is zero, because those have no unmet prerequisites and can safely go first.

I then repeatedly remove a node, append it to the order, and relax each of its outgoing edges by decrementing the neighbour's in-degree, enqueuing a neighbour the moment its in-degree hits zero because all its prerequisites are now placed. The removal order is a valid topological order. The whole algorithm is linear in the number of nodes plus edges. A built-in benefit is cycle detection, because if the final order has fewer nodes than the graph, a cycle prevented some nodes from ever reaching in-degree zero.

At the National Bank of India I used this to order end-of-day batch jobs where interest posting had to precede statement generation and statement generation had to precede archival, so operations needed a run order that never started a job before its prerequisites. I ran Kahn's algorithm over the dependency graph. Explaining the in-degree queue, the relax-on-removal step, and the shortfall-means-cycle check is what shows an interviewer I understand the Topological Sort pattern.
